title: SEBI Says 99.8% of Rajesh Exports' Subsidiary Revenue Was Fabricated. The Number Is ₹15.15 Lakh Crore.
excerpt: India's market regulator has barred the gold exporter and its billionaire chairman from the securities market, alleging the largest revenue inflation in Indian corporate history — routed through a Swiss refinery that actually earned a fraction of what the books claimed.
body:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India has passed an interim order that, if its allegations hold, describes the single largest revenue fabrication in the history of Indian capital markets.

In a 109-page ex parte order dated June 3, SEBI alleged that Bengaluru-based Rajesh Exports — once India's largest gold exporter by reported turnover — inflated its consolidated revenues by approximately ₹15.15 lakh crore over five financial years, from FY21 through FY25. The regulator says that figure represents 99.8 percent of all revenue the company attributed to its overseas subsidiaries during that period.

The order bars Rajesh Exports and its billionaire promoter-chairman Rajesh Mehta from buying, selling, or dealing in the company's securities until further notice. A fresh forensic audit has been ordered.

## The Swiss Connection

At the centre of the case is Valcambi SA, a globally respected Swiss gold refinery that Rajesh Exports acquired in 2015 for $400 million. Valcambi is accredited by the London Bullion Market Association and processes roughly 945 tonnes of gold annually. It is, by all accounts, a legitimate operation.

But between Valcambi and the Indian listed entity sit two intermediate holding companies — REL Singapore and Global Gold Refineries AG (GGR) in Switzerland — with zero employees, zero customers, and zero operations. SEBI alleges that Rajesh Exports used these shell structures to attribute massive revenues to Valcambi that the Swiss refinery never actually generated.

KPMG Switzerland, which audited Valcambi's books, classified the refinery as an *agent* — it processes gold on behalf of clients and earns a processing fee. Valcambi's own audited annual revenues ranged between ₹427 crore and ₹743 crore. In the consolidated accounts of Rajesh Exports, the same operations were attributed ₹2.93 lakh crore of revenue in a single year. That is a gap of 518 times.

## How the Probe Began

The investigation traces back to a shareholder complaint received by SEBI in March 2024. The complainant flagged unusually large trade receivables that had remained unpaid for more than two years — a classic red flag in forensic accounting. SEBI appointed an investigating authority and engaged forensic auditors, who were met with what the regulator describes as systematic non-cooperation.

Key documents were not provided, including records related to customers, vendors, and material subsidiaries. SEBI says the absence of these records made it impossible to verify a significant number of transactions and disclosures.

"The aberrations prima facie noted in the matter — where approx. 97% to 99% of the revenue of the Company is inflated — are egregious and unheard of," the order states.

## The PLI Fallout

The reverberations have already reached the corridors of government. The Ministry of Heavy Industries is reportedly preparing to review Rajesh Exports' inclusion under the Production-Linked Incentive scheme for advanced chemistry cell battery storage. Officials have indicated a strong internal view that the company may be removed from the PLI beneficiary list, with the final decision expected after the Union Minister reviews the SEBI findings.

Rajesh Exports shares, already under pressure before the order was made public, have fallen more than 16 percent month-to-date. The stock hit the 5 percent lower circuit on multiple sessions.

## What It Means for Investors

For NRI investors with exposure to Indian equities — whether directly or through mutual funds that held Rajesh Exports — the case is a stark reminder that reported revenue is only as reliable as the audit trail behind it. Rajesh Exports was, at various points, among the largest companies on Indian exchanges by reported turnover, and its inclusion in indices meant passive fund exposure was inevitable.

Rajesh Mehta has denied all wrongdoing and said the company will resubmit financial documents to SEBI. The promoter's denial notwithstanding, the order stands. The stock remains frozen at circuit limits. And Indian regulators are now asking how a revenue gap of ₹15 lakh crore survived five years of statutory audits without anyone raising the alarm.

The case is sub judice. But the question it has already answered is uncomfortable: India's largest reported gold exporter may have been, in the regulator's telling, India's largest accounting fiction.
